summary: At the Last Supper the apostles argue over who is greatest; Jesus calls Himself the One who serves and promises them a place at His table in His kingdom.
key_insight: Jesus does not end with a rebuke. He tells the very men who had been quarreling, “you are those who have continued with Me in My trials,” and grants them a kingdom. He said this to men who within hours would all forsake Him and flee (Mark 14:50).
story: At the table that last night, a dispute arose among the twelve apostles over “which of them should be considered the greatest.”

Jesus said to them, “The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’ But not so among you.” The greatest among them must become like the younger, and the one who leads like the one who serves.
Then He asked, “For who is greater, he who sits at the table, or he who serves? Is it not he who sits at the table? Yet I am among you as the One who serves.”

He went on, “But you are those who have continued with Me in My trials.” As His Father had bestowed a kingdom on Him, so He bestowed one on them, “that you may eat and drink at My table in My kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

fit.question: Luke tells of the dispute after the bread and the cup and after Jesus’ words about the betrayer (22:14–23). Here, as in McGarvey, Edersheim and many harmonies, it is placed earlier in the evening, before the foot washing. When did the dispute take place?

points.label: At the start of the meal
points.text: McGarvey and Edersheim both set the quarrel at the beginning of the supper. Guests reclined in order of honor, and Jesus had once watched guests choose the best places at a meal (Luke 14:7). On this view He answered the dispute in words (Luke) and in action, rising from supper to wash their feet (John 13:4).

points.label: Luke’s loose link
points.text: Luke opens with “Now there was also a dispute,” words that join the scene to the evening without fixing its moment. He may have gathered Jesus’ sayings at the table about betrayal, greatness, trials and denial into one farewell after the Supper (see also event 150).

points.label: Where Luke puts it
points.text: Others take Luke’s order as the order of events. The apostles’ questioning about which of them would betray Jesus (22:23) turned into a quarrel over which of them was greatest. If so, the argument broke out even after He had washed their feet.

fit.note: Luke does not fix the moment, and either placement keeps every account true; the dispute and Jesus’ answer belong to the same night.
fit.short: Luke’s “Now there was also” does not fix the time. Many place the dispute at the meal’s start; others follow Luke’s order, after the Supper.

scene.label: “Benefactors”
scene.text: Greek kings and Roman rulers liked the title Benefactor, and cities carved it on monuments honoring rulers and wealthy patrons. The Egyptian king Ptolemy III was surnamed Euergetes, which means Benefactor. A benefactor gave gifts and expected honor and loyalty in return.

scene.label: “As the younger”
scene.text: In Jewish society age brought honor and the first place, and the youngest took the humblest tasks. In Acts it is “the young men” who rise to wrap, carry out and bury Ananias (Acts 5:6).

scene.label: Who sits and who serves
scene.text: At a feast the guests reclined while servants stood and waited on them. Jesus had told of a master who says to his servant, “Prepare something for my supper, and gird yourself and serve me” (Luke 17:8). No one at the table doubted which of the two was greater.

scene.label: A seat at the king’s table
scene.text: To eat at a king’s table was a lasting honor. David gave Saul’s grandson Mephibosheth a place at his table “like one of the king’s sons” (2 Samuel 9:11).

scene.label: Thrones for judgment
scene.text: Psalm 122:5 says of Jerusalem, “For thrones are set there for judgment, The thrones of the house of David.” Daniel saw thrones put in place and the kingdom given to “the saints of the Most High” (Daniel 7:9, 27). Matthew records a similar promise of twelve thrones on an earlier day (Matthew 19:28).

witnesses.luke: Only Luke records this dispute at the Supper and Jesus’ answer. Earlier in his Gospel Jesus promised that a returning master would gird himself and serve his watchful servants (12:37), and here the Lord at the table says, “I am among you as the One who serves.” Luke alone gives the word “benefactors,” a title Greek readers knew from public monuments.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the King to whom the Father has given a kingdom, and at His own table He takes the place of the one who serves. He sees the faithfulness of men who are quarreling and about to fail, and He gives them a share in His reign.
seeing.living: The apostles argued about rank at the very table where Jesus was serving them. He did not settle the argument by naming a winner; He pointed to Himself: “I am among you as the One who serves.” Wherever you hope to be noticed or ranked among believers, take the place He took, and leave your honor to the King who has promised His servants a seat at His table.
seeing.ponder: Whose recognition are you still hoping for, and is a seat at Jesus’ table enough for you?

preaching.big_idea: The King who serves at the table promises His servants a place at His own table.
outline: A quarrel at the Lord’s table (24)
A kingdom for those who stayed (28–30)
preaching.watch_for: The table frames the passage: “he who sits at the table” (v. 27) and “eat and drink at My table in My kingdom” (v. 30). The verb “bestow” (v. 29) is related to the Greek word for “covenant” in verse 20, so in Luke’s order the One who has just given the cup of the new covenant now grants His servants a kingdom.
